title: Japanese Curry
subtitle: mild aromatic curry with chicken and vegetables over rice
excerpt: Japanese curry is a thick, mildly spiced sauce with chicken, potato, and carrot served over short-grain rice. It is sweeter and less complex than Indian curry and has become one of Japan's most-loved everyday dishes. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Curry was introduced to Japan via the British Royal Navy in the Meiji period. It evolved into a distinctly Japanese dish with a milder, sweeter flavour profile.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the curry sauce without the rice for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the recipe. The sauce keeps in the fridge for 4 days and improves overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: A block of pre-made Japanese curry seasoning that dissolves into hot broth to create a thick, mild curry sauce. Sold in blocks in Japanese supermarkets.
A sweet, crunchy Japanese relish of pickled vegetables traditionally served alongside Japanese curry rice.

content.text: Japanese curry is thickened with a
block that dissolves into the cooking liquid and creates a glossy, thick sauce. The result is mild and slightly sweet. Serve with
pickles on the side for crunch. Serves 4.
Japanese curry roux comes in mild, medium, and hot. Use mild for children or anyone new to the dish. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon.

items.prepNote: peeled and cut into 3 cm chunks

content.text: Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes, stirring often, until golden and softened.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for 1 minute. Add the chicken pieces and brown lightly on all sides, about 4 minutes.
Add the carrot and potato. Pour in 800 ml of water and bring to the boil. Reduce heat and simmer for 15 minutes until the vegetables are just tender.
Break the curry roux block into pieces and stir into the hot liquid until fully dissolved and the sauce is thick. Add soy sauce. Simmer for 5 more minutes.
Cook the rice separately in a medium saucepan. Serve the curry alongside a mound of rice, with the sauce ladled over.

attrs.symptom: Sauce is lumpy after adding the roux
attrs.cause: The roux was added to a liquid that was not hot enough or stirred too quickly.
attrs.fix: Take the pot off the heat, add roux pieces, and stir slowly as you return it to low heat.

attrs.symptom: Potatoes are falling apart and the curry looks starchy
attrs.cause: The potatoes cooked too long before the roux was added.
attrs.fix: Add roux as soon as the vegetables are just tender. The sauce thickens fast.

attrs.cause: The onion was not cooked long enough to develop sweetness.
attrs.fix: Cook the onion until deep golden, at least 8 minutes. This is the flavour base of the whole dish.

content.text: Japanese curry arrived via the British navy in the Meiji era. Japan adapted it heavily and made it sweeter, thicker, and milder than its South Asian origins. Today it is one of the most frequently cooked weeknight meals in Japan. School canteens serve it on Fridays. Naval officers still eat curry every Friday as a naval tradition. It is deeply embedded in everyday Japanese life.
